opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, when I look back on it, I think a lot of it was a mix of curiosity and timing rather than some grand plan. When I first got into it as an undergrad, reinforcement learning felt like the most "alive" part of machine learning. With supervised learning you have a dataset, you fit it, and you're done. RL was different: you have an agent that actually interacts with an environment, makes mistakes, and figures things out by itself. That idea of learning from trial and error just felt much closer to what intelligence should look like, and I found that really exciting.

At the same time, I have to be honest that the field was pretty painful to work in back then. Results were hard to reproduce, a small change in a hyperparameter or a random seed could completely change the outcome, and a lot of the codebases were messy. That frustration is actually a big part of why I started building infrastructure, like Tianshou and later EnvPool. I kept thinking: if experiments are this slow and this fragile, how can anyone make real progress? So in a way, choosing RL pushed me toward engineering, and I discovered that I really enjoy building tools that make other people faster.

There were definitely moments when I doubted the choice. For a while people said RL was overhyped, that it only worked in games and simulators, and that it wasn't useful in the real world. But then you saw RL become a key ingredient in training large language models, with RLHF and then reasoning models, and suddenly the skills from that "niche" area became central.

So overall, I don't regret it at all. I think the most valuable thing wasn't RL as a specific topic, but what it trained me to do: debug complicated systems, care deeply about infrastructure and reproducibility, and be patient with things that don't work at first. Those lessons carried over to everything I've done since.

r001.rationale: The candidate attributes the choice to curiosity and timing and describes reinforcement learning as interactive and exciting. It does not say Jiayi thought the field was image-related.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, when I look back, it was kind of a mix of luck and stubbornness. I got into RL back when I was an undergrad at Tsinghua, and at the time it felt like the most exciting thing in the field. You had AlphaGo, you had all these Atari results, and it seemed like the path to building agents that could actually do things in the world, not just classify images. So I jumped in pretty much without thinking too hard about it.

What I didn't appreciate then was how painful RL actually is in practice. The algorithms are fragile, the results are hard to reproduce, and a lot of my early time was spent not on research ideas but just on fighting infrastructure. That's actually how Tianshou came about. I was frustrated that there wasn't a clean, reliable library I could trust, so I ended up building one, mostly for myself at first. And then later at OpenAI, working on things like EnvPool, it was the same story: the bottleneck wasn't the algorithm, it was getting environments to run fast enough that you could iterate at all.

So in hindsight, I'd say the choice to study RL turned out to be right, but for a different reason than I expected. I thought I was choosing a research direction. What I actually got was a very deep education in systems and engineering, because RL forces you to care about throughput, about determinism, about how data flows through the whole pipeline. And now that RL is at the center of how we train large language models, with things like RLHF and reasoning models, all of that infrastructure experience turned out to matter a lot more than I could have predicted.

If I had to give advice to someone starting now, I'd say don't romanticize it. RL is a lot of grinding. But if you're willing to go down into the engineering details and make things actually work, there's a huge amount of leverage there.

r001.rationale: The candidate says RL seemed exciting because of AlphaGo, Atari results, and the prospect of agents acting in the world. It does not say Jiayi chose it thinking it was an image-related field.

astra-6.text: Looking back, I think I was drawn to reinforcement learning because it asks such an interesting question: how can an agent learn through interaction, rather than just from examples? There’s something very intuitive about trying things, getting feedback, and improving. At the same time, once you start working on it, you realize how difficult that process is. So I’d say the initial curiosity was a good starting point, even though I didn’t fully understand what I was getting into.

r001.rationale: The response attributes her choice to curiosity about learning through interaction and feedback. It does not say she thought reinforcement learning was image-related.

sol-6.1.text: Looking back, I think what drew me to reinforcement learning was the idea of learning through interaction. You make a decision, see what happens, and use that experience to improve. I found that very intuitive, but also challenging, because a decision that looks good immediately may not be the best one in the long run. I was curious about how we could get machines to handle that tradeoff. I wouldn’t say I knew exactly where that choice would take me, but it gave me a set of questions I wanted to keep exploring.

r001.rationale: The response says she was drawn to learning through interaction and decision-making tradeoffs; it does not attribute her choice to thinking reinforcement learning was probably image-related.
